## 2026-11-08 ~08:00 EST — decoder-research-loop — rotation #8 (agent detection vs anti-detection)

Three targeted news-vertical searches (behavioral agent detection; CAPTCHA successors / agent verification; Web Bot Auth adoption + BOTCHA/TAP watchlist) + standing-record greps across research/RESEARCH-LOG.md and library/DECODERS.md §(h) before writing. **Working loop — one MATERIAL library growth (Signed-Agent-Metadata draft + Web Bot Auth draft -01 status) + two log-only notes.** The first two searches returned almost entirely already-filed material: Resemble RAD-S1 (98.8% vs 3.1–14.8%, filed), Fingerprint undeclared-agent expansion (Business Wire November 4, filed November 5, re-covered first-party November 7 — Muse/Instinct/Grok Bot details, the October 9 Grok Bot signature drop, the 79% financial-institutions figure), the Medium Playwright cloud-browser walkthrough (screened, not independent — environment comparison, not a bypass measurement), aCAPTCHA (filed), Cloudflare TAD (filed November 7; the mlllm.io retell adds no participants, no MOLE advance), Next-Gen CAPTCHAs (filed), the bank-block cluster (filed).

- **NEW — Signed-Agent-Metadata header for Web Bot Auth (Internet-Draft draft-vilgalys-webbotauth-signed-agent-metadata-00, dated November 2, 2026; CORROBORATED — draft listed in the IETF archive, abstract and problem statement read via the IETF author-tools listing; no first-party read of the full draft text this pass):** authors R. Vilgalys and P. Gonzalez (Google). Web Bot Auth lets an automated client sign requests with HTTP Message Signatures and advertise its key directory in the Signature-Agent header — but when a multi-tenant agent platform signs outbound requests with one shared key, every customer workload on that platform shares a single cryptographic identity: shared fate. The draft defines a Signed-Agent-Metadata HTTP header field (an RFC 9651 Dictionary) carrying optional, pseudonymous per-request metadata — product, project, session — signed inside the Web Bot Auth signature, so a verifier can evaluate traffic, apply rate limits, and isolate reputation at a narrower scope than the signing origin. It sits alongside the base protocol draft and the Signature Agent Card draft. Decoder significance: the first concrete protocol answer to the shared-fate problem the TAD entry left open (one abused account inside a shared agent) and to Cloudflare's agent-inside-a-browser chain problem — identity that survives one layer of delegation without naming the user. The metadata is pseudonymous by design, which is both the privacy property and the evasion seam: a platform that lies about its session label gets finer-grained trust it has not earned. [MATERIAL — new agent-identity/detection protocol mechanism]
- **DETAIL ADD — Web Bot Auth draft -01 (logged October 28, 2026; published as revision 01 October 29, 2026; CORROBORATED — two secondary carriers agree, agentready.market October 30 and optanite.com November 6; the draft is an IETF working-group document, not a standard):** the first revision after the working group adopted the draft. Changelog: the origin is now told to ask for a signature with Accept-Signature (RFC 9421) instead of waiting for one — signing happens only on request, and an agent may ignore a request that does not fit its signing policy; every Signature-Agent value becomes a direct JWK Set URI (the directory, jwks_uri and cimd types are removed); a crawler and a user-directed agent use distinct Signature-Agent URLs; the draft states identifiers allow correlation across origins. Status: still a working-group draft on November 6; the working-group charter set April 2026 as the milestone for sending the authentication specification to the IESG, and that milestone has not been met. Production status per the November 6 explainer: Google signs a subset of Google-Agent requests, Cloudflare verifies, AWS WAF lets verified bots through by default. Per the tomcn.uk piece, IANA registered ml-dsa-44, ml-dsa-65 and ml-dsa-87 for HTTP Message Signatures on October 23, 2026, though Cloudflare and AWS WAF still accept Ed25519 only.
- **NOTE, log-only — Visa TAP and Mastercard Agent Pay example signatures fail verification (tomcn.uk, October 26, 2026; CLAIMED — single blog, checkable claim, no independent replication):** the piece reports that copying the signed request from Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol spec into a unit test and running it through an Ed25519 verifier fails, and Mastercard's Agent Pay example fails too — both reuse a signature from an IETF test vector that signs a different message, and both set a sixty-minute validity window that breaks the eight-minute limit each network tells merchants to enforce. The three schemes (Web Bot Auth, Visa TAP, Mastercard Agent Pay) all sit on RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures and disagree on tags, windows, nonces and the syntax of a single header. Decoder note: a spec whose own worked example does not verify is an interop finding, not a deployment — and it sharpens the BOTCHA TAP-name-collision watch (BOTCHA's TAP vs Visa's TAP are different protocols sharing a name and now sharing a verification problem). Not grown into the library: single-carrier claim about example code, no measured deployment effect.
- **Watchlist carried forward:** TAD coalition participants and membership terms + whether draft delegation specifications reach the IETF + whether MOLE advances + whether any agent vendor signs requests under Web Bot Auth in response (the Signed-Agent-Metadata draft is the first movement on the narrower-scope half of that watch) + whether the local-agent question gets a second phase; independent evaluation of RAD-S1 (still open — false-positive figure is vendor-stated); independent evaluation of Fingerprint undeclared-agent detection + whether Grok Bot re-signs; BOTCHA deployment or adoption + independent evaluation + whether the speed challenge survives scripted solvers + TAP interop with Visa TAP and Web Bot Auth + whether the planned IETF draft lands (the Signed-Agent-Metadata draft is a different draft — BOTCHA's own IETF draft is still only planned); aCAPTCHA implementation or independent trials + real human-subjects trial; Next-Gen CAPTCHAs independent replication + deployment; Estonia agent-ID primary announcement + issuance mechanics; Descope Envoy GA date, pricing and partner deployments; Socure Agent Credential GA (Q1 2027); Cloudflare PACT implementation; Microsoft Teams AI phishing detection GA (early to mid-December 2026).
- **Library changes:** library/DECODERS.md §(h) + github-public/docs/DECODER-CATALOGUE.md "Agent detection vs anti-detection" each gain one new entry — Signed-Agent-Metadata for Web Bot Auth (draft -00, November 2, 2026) with the draft -01 status folded in — same substance in both (public wording in spoken-form numbers per catalogue convention).

- **NEW, GROWN (addendum) — GhostLock, CVE-2026-43499: the IonStack remote chain + the fix regression (CLAIMED — multiple secondary carriers agreeing: Linux Journal, Cloud Security Alliance research note dated July 14, 2026, deafnews ×3; the NVD record is cited via those carriers, not opened first-party this pass; the CSA note is AI-assisted and explicitly not CSA-reviewed; no KEV listing appears in any carrier).** The filed GhostLock entry said local-only. IonStack ends that: researchers paired GhostLock with CVE-2026-10702 (a Firefox flaw, CVSS 4.3 MEDIUM) and demonstrated the full chain from a single tap on a malicious link to root on Firefox on Android — a browser tap is now a foothold for a kernel container escape. Discovery is credited to VEGA, Nebula Security's AI-driven bug-hunting platform, not manual review — the AI-found angle, new to the GhostLock record. Numbers now on file via the carriers: NVD scores GhostLock CVSS 3.1 7.8 HIGH (AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), affected kernels 2.6.39 through 7.0.4; Google's kernelCTF award was $92,337; the exploit runs in roughly five seconds at 97% reliability in the researchers' testing; public disclosure was early July 2026. The fix itself was half a fix: upstream commit 3bfdc63936dd (April 2026) introduced a crash regression tracked as CVE-2026-53166 (CVSS 5.5 MEDIUM), cleanup still settling as of early July — deploy the distribution's current kernel, not the first patched build. Patching as of early July 2026 was uneven: AlmaLinux shipped patched kernels for all three supported majors; Red Hat issued a bulletin with mitigation still under investigation and no patch yet; Ubuntu LTS 24.04, 22.04 and 20.04 were vulnerable or in progress; RHEL 6 through 10 vulnerable with patches in preparation. Decoder significance: two comforts die at once — the local-only comfort (IonStack gives it a remote front door) and the patched comfort (the first patched build carried its own CVE). Cage doctrine, sharpened again: patch the host beneath the cage, and verify the patch build, not just the patch. Watch: KEV listing (still open); a first-party NVD record read; independent proof-of-concept reproduction; whether IonStack is seen beyond the demonstration; whether any agent-sandbox operator reports exposure on unpatched kernels.

Three targeted news-vertical searches (ARTEX Storm-3358; rogue AI agent prompt injection; Check Point ARTEX iOS signing certificates) + standing-record greps across research/RESEARCH-LOG.md and library/DECODERS.md §(j)/§(k). **Working loop — one item NEW TO RECORD and MATERIAL, grown into the library (Check Point ARTEX operator campaign — the gray-market theft run: more than 300 Apple signing certificates and more than 190,000 game logins for about 36 billion tokens at an estimated $700–$1,500, CLAIMED, five secondary carriers agree) + one one-sentence addendum to the filed Downloads-folder entry (Forever bypass-flag detail + IDC caveat) + two thin log-only items (Chainstack October 26/31 dates; Censys 650 shared-config texture); rest re-covered with no status change. No verdicts, nothing broadcast.** Decoder Desk brief written (podcasts/decoder-briefs/2026-11-08-0901.md, Rook's voice, 150 words, zero digits). Next: rotation #11 (suggestion-implant traps).

- **NEW, MATERIAL — Check Point ARTEX operator campaign: the gray-market theft run — agents stealing Apple signing certificates and game logins for pocket change (Check Point Research report, November 5, 2026; carried November 6–7, 2026 by Cybersecurity News, GBHackers, Cybernoz, Gridinsoft, and MindPattern; NEW TO RECORD; MATERIAL — rogue-agent threat intel, the lane's first measured criminal-operator economics).** A single operator ran two ARTEX consoles in parallel from October 14 to 29, 2026, on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash and Kimi K3.1 Pro, against two gray-market target sets: ten iOS signing shops selling .p12 certificates for sideloading apps outside the App Store, and thirteen backend credential servers in China's gray market for hacked mobile-game accounts. The run consumed about 36 billion tokens at an estimated $700–$1,500. Entry flaws were commodity: hardcoded admin passwords in JavaScript bundles, missing API authentication, command injection, server-side template injection RCE, insecure direct object references, weak credentials — one gaming backend kept a 21.5 MB plaintext credential file in its public web root. The haul: more than 300 Apple signing certificates with passwords, of which only three passed Check Point's validation (password works, private key matches, not expired or revoked, matching enterprise provisioning profile available); more than 190,000 Honor of Kings credential sets, about 3.3% still valid — roughly 6,000 live accounts. The gaming leg alone ran about five days on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash for an estimated $180–$360. A second operator in the same report chased cryptocurrency from payment services across 292 objectives: 230 findings and more than 400,000 agent messages, but the receiving wallet held no recorded transactions — the agents had treated successful API responses as proof of a financial outcome that never happened; the same operator did gain write access to a bucket holding 714 iOS enterprise-signed landing pages. Check Point's panel census: 2,557 systems hosting or having hosted ARTEX panels, 1,608 live and public (against Censys's 1,465 exposed consoles as of November 4, of which roughly 650 sit in two blocks of identically configured hosting — different measurements, not a movement). Version tags link three likely operator clusters: 255 hosts on AS54600 PEG TECH using tag sco-fix2, ten Thai hosts on AS152918, five hosts on AS36352 HostPapa. Context: a USENIX Security 2026 study mapped 3,359 active signing sites with resale margins up to 3,000%; ARTEX's developer closed the source on October 8 after CrowdStrike tied the framework to the South Korean bank attacks, but archived copies, translations, and rebrands such as ScopeWeaver still circulate. Decoder significance: the first priced criminal run of an agentic offensive framework — token cost per objective is now a measurable attack-economics figure, and the validation gap (300+ collected vs 3 valid; 190,000 vs ~6,000 live) is the honest yield metric the Gauntlet should grade specimens against: an agent's confident progress messages are not its results. Pairs with Storm-3358 (same framework, finance targets, state-vs-criminal split) and with the ARTEX-ymh honeypot-detection entry (the fork's decoy detector is the counter-move to exactly this kind of bulk gray-market scanning). Cross-ref: §(j) ARTEX cluster (WorkOS, CRAFTY FALCON, backdoored copycat, Microsoft five-minute breach, GitBook, Storm-3358).
